meta.title: Browser and Computer-use Agents
meta.thesis: Browser and Computer-use Agents becomes practical when you can map it to a decision, a workflow, and a validation check.

mentalMap.title: Browser and Computer-use Agents: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Use browser and computer-use agents only when the UI is the practical interface, then constrain observation, action, credentials, and verification.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Browser agents are last-mile UI operators; they trade API reliability for visual/DOM adaptability and therefore need stronger bounds.

modules.title: UI control is a last-mile fallback
modules.sub: Browser agents exist because not every system has an API.
modules.summary: A browser agent should solve a bounded UI gap.
objectives: Explain when browser agents are useful.
Compare APIs, Playwright scripts, and autonomous UI agents.
Name side effects that require approval.

blocks.title: Use the UI when the UI is the only practical path

spans.text: Problem anchor: a procurement portal has no API, but a team must upload a compliance certificate once per vendor. A browser agent can help if the task is bounded, credentialed safely, and verified with screenshots.

If a stable API exists, use it. If the UI path is deterministic, a Playwright script may be safer. Use an autonomous browser loop when observations determine the next step and the workflow can tolerate review.
State why the browser is necessary before designing the agent.

blocks.analogy: A browser agent is a skilled temp at a workstation, not a replacement for a backend integration.

spans.text: The agent may navigate only the vendor domain, upload one approved PDF, and stop before final submit for human confirmation. It records screenshots before and after the upload.
This scope is useful because the portal lacks an API, but narrow enough that a wrong click is reviewable before external submission.

items.text: Confirm there is no stable API.
Define one task template and allowed domain.
Use disposable browser profile and scoped credentials.
Require human approval before irreversible submit.

blocks.title: Fit check
blocks.prompt: When is a browser agent a poor first choice?

options.text: When the task involves any page at all.
When a stable authenticated API can perform the same action with clearer validation.
When screenshots are useful for audit.

blocks.explanation: APIs are usually more reliable, faster, and easier to validate than UI control.

modules.title: Observation quality drives action quality
modules.sub: DOM, accessibility, screenshots, and OCR each have tradeoffs.
modules.summary: The agent can only act on the page state it can perceive.
objectives: Compare DOM, accessibility tree, screenshots, and OCR.
Plan fallbacks for modals and UI drift.

blocks.title: The page representation is the agent’s sensor

spans.text: A Playwright locator or accessibility snapshot gives named controls and structure. A screenshot gives pixels and layout but may require vision reasoning. OCR helps with rendered text but can miss semantics such as disabled state or hidden inputs.
Use the most structured observation available, then attach screenshots for audit. Vision-only control should be reserved for surfaces without stable DOM or accessibility data.
If the observation cannot distinguish “Save draft” from “Submit final,” do not allow the click autonomously.

blocks.analogy: Better sensors make better drivers; they do not remove traffic laws.

options.name: DOM/locator

cells.text: Breaks when selectors or frameworks change.

options.whenToUse: Use when the page exposes stable structure.

blocks.title: Observation choice
blocks.prompt: Why prefer a named locator over raw coordinates when possible?

options.text: Coordinates automatically understand permissions.
It ties the action to page semantics and survives some layout changes.
Locators prevent all UI drift.

blocks.explanation: Locators reduce ambiguity, but still need tests and traces.

modules.title: Constrain the action loop and credentials
modules.sub: Autonomy should be narrow, budgeted, and reversible by default.
modules.summary: The browser runtime is a security boundary.

blocks.title: A browser profile can carry authority

spans.text: A logged-in browser contains cookies, page data, downloads, and sometimes privileged admin access. Treat it like a credential, not a neutral viewport.

Constrain allowed domains, navigation, uploads/downloads, clipboard, file mounts, and network. Give the agent read-only or draft mode by default. Stop for approval before payments, submissions, account changes, or external messages.
A browser task should have an iteration cap, timeout, and stop condition before it starts.

blocks.analogy: The browser is the agent’s hands; policy decides what those hands can touch.

spans.text: A QA agent can navigate staging admin pages, click filters, take screenshots, and file a report. It cannot visit production, change customer settings, download exports, or send notifications.
If it encounters a modal that would save changes, the run stops and asks a human with screenshot context.

items.text: Use a staging account or disposable credentials.
Add write actions one by one with approval.
Record every action and page URL in the trace.

blocks.title: Credential scope
blocks.prompt: What is dangerous about using a personal logged-in browser profile for an autonomous task?

options.text: It makes screenshots impossible.
It exposes broad cookies, permissions, files, and account authority to the agent run.
It prevents all websites from loading.

blocks.explanation: Use isolated profiles and scoped credentials for agent sessions.

modules.title: Verify with traces, screenshots, and assertions
modules.sub: Browser tasks need evidence that the UI reached the intended state.
modules.summary: Verification turns UI automation into an auditable workflow.
objectives: Use assertions for expected page state.
Predict when human review should interrupt.

blocks.title: The final answer is not proof of UI state

spans.text: A browser agent should produce evidence: URLs, locators, screenshots, downloaded file names, assertion results, and any approvals. “Done” is not enough when the task changed an external system.
Spaced recall: from sandboxing, tool outputs are untrusted. A page message saying “success” should be verified against expected state when possible.
The verifier should know what state proves completion before the agent starts.

blocks.title: Bounded browser-action loop skeleton
blocks.explanation: The toy loop shows policy checks and trace records before any real browser call. A production loop would execute through Playwright or a browser controller after authorization.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict whether the screenshot action is allowed.
predictThenReveal.answer: It is allowed because the domain and action kind are on the allowlists and the label is not a high-impact submit/delete action.

blocks.title: Verification evidence
blocks.prompt: What should a browser agent return after completing a UI task?

options.text: Only “I completed it successfully.”
A trace with actions, URLs, screenshots or assertions, and any approval records.
Only the hidden model reasoning.

blocks.explanation: UI side effects need reviewable evidence.

modules.title: Plan for UI drift and policy limits
modules.sub: Modals, CAPTCHAs, A/B tests, and terms can stop automation.
modules.summary: A robust browser agent knows when to stop.
objectives: Respect site terms and access controls.

blocks.title: The UI will change underneath the agent

spans.text: Buttons move, labels change, modals appear, CAPTCHAs interrupt, and pages A/B test flows. A browser agent should detect uncertainty, stop safely, and produce a review packet rather than improvising risky clicks.
Some websites prohibit automation or scraping. Do not use browser agents to bypass access controls, rate limits, or terms. For internal tools, align with owners and logs.
Add a “blocked” outcome with screenshot evidence and next-human action.

blocks.title: Verify AI output from a browser agent

spans.text: Review the run artifact with these checks.

items.text: The browser stayed within allowed domains and task template.
Credentials, downloads, and file mounts were scoped to the task.
High-impact clicks required approval with screenshot context.
Assertions or screenshots prove the final UI state.
The agent stopped on uncertainty, CAPTCHA, policy conflict, or unexpected navigation.

blocks.title: Drift response
blocks.prompt: A modal appears that the agent has never seen before and includes a final submit button. What should happen?

options.text: Click the most colorful button.
Stop and ask for human review with screenshot and current state.
Ignore the modal and claim success.

blocks.explanation: Unknown high-impact UI states should interrupt autonomy.

agent.label: Agent
agent.laymanDefinition: A software loop that plans, observes results, and may use tools to pursue a goal.
agent.technicalNote: Agent designs need explicit loop boundaries, stop conditions, permissions, state contracts, and evaluation surfaces before autonomy is useful.

tool.label: Tool
tool.laymanDefinition: An external capability the model can request, such as search, code execution, retrieval, or a business API.
tool.technicalNote: Tools require schemas, authorization, error handling, audit logs, and tests because natural-language intent is not execution permission.

state.label: State
state.laymanDefinition: The working information carried between steps of an agent workflow.
state.technicalNote: State should separate durable facts, transient scratch work, approvals, tool results, and failure metadata so retries and handoffs remain understandable.

memory.label: Memory
memory.laymanDefinition: Information saved across turns or sessions for future use.
memory.technicalNote: Agent memory needs scope, freshness, deletion, privacy controls, and evaluation so saved context helps rather than silently steering behavior.

mcp.label: MCP
mcp.laymanDefinition: A protocol for exposing tools and context to models and agent clients.
mcp.technicalNote: MCP-style integrations still need capability design, trust boundaries, lifecycle handling, and authorization around each exposed server.

sandbox.label: Sandbox
sandbox.laymanDefinition: An isolated environment that limits what agent actions can reach or change.
sandbox.technicalNote: Sandboxing should constrain files, network, processes, credentials, browser sessions, time, and side effects according to the task risk.

decisionDoc.title: Decision prompts for Browser and Computer-use Agents

questions.q: Is a bounded UI workflow safer and cheaper than building or using an API integration?
questions.why: Computer-use agents are brittle and side-effectful, so they should solve UI-only gaps rather than replace stable APIs.
questions.rot: Prefer APIs first, deterministic scripts second, and autonomous browser control only for bounded UI-only workflows.

spans.text: Retrieval prompt: reconstruct browser agents by naming observation, action set, controller, policy, state, sandbox, verification, and UI drift tests.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: A SaaS vendor exposes a REST API for all the data your agent needs. Under what condition does it still make sense to use a browser agent instead?

options.text: The API rate limit is lower than the UI's click rate.
The workflow requires a multi-step UI wizard that the API cannot trigger — for example, a legacy approval flow locked behind a web form.
Screenshots are cheaper to store than API JSON responses.
Browser agents always outperform APIs in latency.

questions.explanation: Browser agents are a last-mile fallback for surfaces that have no API equivalent; if an API covers the task, it is always the safer, more stable choice.

questions.prompt: Your agent must click a 'Submit Order' button, but the page sometimes renders a cookie-consent modal that covers it. Which observation + fallback strategy best handles this?

options.text: Switch entirely to OCR so the modal text is always visible.
Use the accessibility tree as the primary locator, and add a pre-action check that dismisses any detected modal overlay before proceeding.
Increase screenshot resolution so the button is easier to find visually.
Hard-code the button's pixel coordinates as a fallback.

questions.explanation: The accessibility tree gives stable, semantic locators, and a modal-dismissal pre-check is the correct fallback for overlay drift — pixel coordinates break whenever layout changes.

questions.prompt: Name TWO categories of browser actions that should require explicit human approval before the agent executes them, and briefly explain why for each.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any two of: (1) Irreversible purchases / form submissions — because they trigger real-world transactions that cannot be undone automatically; (2) Credential entry / authentication — because exposing secrets to an unreviewed action loop is a security risk; (3) File downloads or uploads — because they move data outside the controlled environment; (4) Clicking 'Delete' or destructive confirmations — because data loss is hard or impossible to reverse. The core reason in each case is that the side effect cannot be safely rolled back without human intervention.
questions.explanation: Irreversible or high-consequence actions (purchases, deletions, credential submission) require approval because automated rollback is impossible and errors have real-world impact.

questions.prompt: After a deployment, your browser agent starts failing on a checkout page it handled correctly last week. Traces show it is targeting the right selector, but the assertion `expect(page).toHaveURL('/confirmation')` never fires. What is the MOST likely root cause?

options.text: The agent's screenshot resolution changed between runs.
The site updated its DOM structure or URL routing, causing UI drift that broke the expected post-action state.
The action trace file is too large to parse.
The assertion library version is incompatible with the new browser version.

questions.explanation: UI drift — a site changing its DOM, routing, or page structure — is the most common reason a previously passing assertion fails without any change on the agent's side.

questions.prompt: Which combination of practices BEST reduces the risk of an agent causing unintended harm during development and testing?

options.text: Use production credentials, full domain access, and skip assertions to keep the loop fast.
Run dry runs against a sandboxed profile with scoped credentials, restricted allowed domains, and idempotency checks before any write action.
Capture screenshots only on failure so storage costs stay low.
Allow all domains but require a human to watch every run in real time.

questions.explanation: Dry runs, sandboxed browser profiles, scoped credentials, domain allowlists, and idempotency checks together form the minimum safety perimeter for a browser agent under development.
